title: TypeScript with React
subtitle: Props interfaces, useState<T>, useRef<T>, event types, and React.FC
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: React components have no enforcement on what props they accept. Passing the wrong prop type, using the wrong event type, or forgetting a required prop are common bugs in plain JavaScript React.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript + React: define an interface for component props, annotate useState with its value type, use React's typed event types for handlers. The result: component contracts that TypeScript enforces at every call site.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every React project in production should use TypeScript. Type checking catches prop typos and wrong types before runtime. IDEs provide full autocomplete for props, events, and React APIs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Quick throwaway prototypes or examples where you just want to move fast. Switch to TypeScript before the code grows.

explainModes.beginner: In React with TypeScript, you describe what 'ingredients' a component needs using an interface. TypeScript then checks every place you use that component — if you forget a required prop or pass the wrong type, it's an error before you even open the browser.
explainModes.simple: Props interface: interface Props { label: string; count?: number }. Component: function Btn({ label }: Props) { ... }. useState: useState<number>(0) — value is number, setter expects number | (prev: number) => number. useRef: useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) — ref.current is HTMLInputElement | null. Events: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>.
explainModes.standard: React.FC<Props> is a function component type. It automatically includes children in props and infers the return type as JSX.Element. Modern best practice (React 18+): prefer plain function + return type annotation over React.FC, since React.FC has some tricky behaviors (children used to be implicit in older React). Event handler type: (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => void. React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> for form submit.
explainModes.technical: JSX.Element vs React.ReactNode vs React.ReactElement: JSX.Element is the return type of JSX expressions. React.ReactNode is the wider type (anything that can be rendered: string, number, null, JSX). Use React.ReactNode for children type. React.ComponentPropsWithRef<'button'> extracts all HTML button attributes — spread them with your extras: interface ButtonProps extends React.ComponentPropsWithRef<'button'> { label: string }. useReducer generic: useReducer<Reducer<State, Action>>(reducer, initialState).
explainModes.deepDive: Generic components: function Select<T>({ options, onSelect }: { options: T[]; onSelect: (v: T) => void }) — component is parameterized by the option type. Context with TypeScript: createContext requires a type and a default: const Ctx = createContext<User | null>(null). Custom hooks: function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string): [T | null, (val: T) => void] — typed hook. forwardRef: const Input = forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, InputProps>((props, ref) => ...) — typed ref forwarding. Type-safe routing with react-router-dom: useParams<{ id: string }>() — params are typed.

questions.question: What is the correct type for `useState` when managing a `User | null` state?
questions.explanation: useState<User | null>(null) is correct. The generic type parameter tells TypeScript what types the state can hold. With User | null, the setter accepts User, null, or a function (prev: User | null) => User | null. If you wrote useState<User>(null), TypeScript would error — null is not assignable to User (with strictNullChecks). If you wrote useState(null), TypeScript would infer the type as null — and you'd never be able to set a User.

faq.q: Should I use React.FC or plain function components?
faq.a: Modern React (18+) best practice: use plain function components with an explicit props interface. React.FC<Props> is fine but has some quirks (it used to include children implicitly, which is not always wanted). Plain function syntax is more explicit: function Button({ label }: ButtonProps): JSX.Element { ... } — the props and return type are clear. Most modern React codebases avoid React.FC.
